Across the whole model, a2 = 2 instead of 3 raises it, while the typical case stays below 1%.

parts.name: two_indicator_band
parts.original_hypothesis: Output = sigmoid(Ramp - 1.20 - 5.64*Gate): an additive composition under the output sigmoid. Unconnected inputs a2:2, a4:2, a4:3, a5:2, a5:3 and a5:4 are zero-effect entries; the model never consults them. When no indicator is active the gate is about 13, and its -5.64 readout overwhelms the ramp (logit about -54). With one active indicator the gate still wins (logit <= -8.96). With two, the gate is (almost) off and the logit equals the ramp, -3.34 to +5.63. With three or more, the ramp itself is <= -3.41. So the network produces a peak at count two of the six rule indicators. The ramp makes the upper edge and the gate makes the lower edge: the mirror image of a single gate plus ramp construction. Because the ramp weights are uneven, the peak is not level. Pairs involving a6=1 (with a1, a2, a4 or a5) get logits -3.34 to -1.07 and fall below p=0.5, and so do some a2&a4 and a4&a5 configurations; a3&a6 stays positive because I3 is light. Train evidence (n=345): AUC 1.0, since every count-2 logit (>= -3.337) exceeds every other logit (<= -3.408), a margin of only 0.07. Accuracy at 0.5 is 0.890: 38 false negatives, all count-2 rows, and no false positives. Local ablation with the gate set to 0 drops train accuracy to 0.632 and turns every count<=1 row positive.

parts.name: few_indicators_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: A fewer-than-two-indicators gate. Write I_k = 1 when attribute k takes its first value (a3:2 = 1-I3 and a6:2 = 1-I6, since a3 and a6 are binary). In these terms node 217 computes ReLU(13.02 - 8.77 I1 - 7.32 I2 - 6.57 I3 - 6.43 I4 - 9.36 I5 - 7.15 I6 - 0.20[a1=3] + 0.39[a2=3]), a near-uniform weighted count of active indicators (weights 6.4 to 9.4) subtracted from 13. It outputs about 13 when no indicator is active, 3.5 to 7.0 when exactly one is, and zero once two or more are. The one leak: the lightest pair (I3+I4) leaves at most +0.41, so the gate fires weakly on 6% of count-2 configurations. Evidence (train, n=345): node 217 ranges 12.82-13.40 at count 0, 3.46-6.98 at count 1, 0-0.41 at count 2, and exactly 0 at count>=3; sensitivities are about 0.8-1.15 for the six indicator columns and about 0.03-0.05 for a1:3 and a2:3, which are negligible.

parts.name: descending_count_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: A descending linear count ramp. The direct input-to-output connections sum, in rule-indicator terms, to 20.80 - 8.72 I1 - 9.45 I2 - 5.25 I3 - 10.01 I4 - 9.04 I5 - 11.95 I6 - 0.53[a1=2] - 0.45[a2=3]. a3 and a6 enter through both of their one-hot columns, which combine into single indicator weights. Each active indicator subtracts 5 to 12, and the weights are not uniform: I6 is heaviest (11.95) and I3 lightest (5.25). With the output bias (-1.20) the ramp is +18.6 to +19.6 at count 0, +6.7 to +14.4 at count 1, -3.3 to +5.6 at count 2, and at most -3.41 at every count>=3 (train). It forms the upper edge of the response: three or more active indicators always switch the output off. Evidence: closed form, plus per-count ranges on the train split (n=345).

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_25.text: This part acts on 95 of 345 training cases (28%).
For a typical case it acts on, it clearly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without this part to below 1% with it.
In the training data, 6 of these 95 cases had 'yes'.
For a typical case, going from a5 = 1 to attribute a5 other than a5 = 1 moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 2% to about 99% if a6 = 2, and from below 1% to below 1% if a6 = 1.
Other effects: a1 depending on a6 lowers it; a1 depending on a5 lowers it.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: any other attribute a5 (rather than a5 = 1) lowers it; a1 = 2 (rather than a1 = 1) lowers it; a1 = 3 (rather than a1 = 1) lowers it; a1 depending on a2 lowers it; a2 = 1 (rather than a2 = 3) raises it; a6 = 2 (rather than a6 = 1) lowers it; a3 = 2 (rather than a3 = 1) lowers it; a4 = 1 (rather than any other attribute a4) raises it; and one still smaller effect listed in the evidence table.

ann_26.text: Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a6 = 2 (rather than a6 = 1) raises it; any other attribute a5 (rather than a5 = 1) raises it; a1 = 3 (rather than a1 = 1) raises it; a1 = 2 (rather than a1 = 1) raises it; a3 = 2 (rather than a3 = 1) raises it; a4 = 1 (rather than any other attribute a4) lowers it; a2 = 1 (rather than a2 = 3) lowers it; a2 = 2 (rather than a2 = 3) raises it.

ann_27.text: For a typical case, the model gives a slightly higher predicted probability of 'yes' if a2 = 2 (below 1%) than if a2 = 3 (below 1%).
